rv.q: In performance and direction, and in the small ways in which Caswell and Wills have plotted out this isolated love story, there's a level of great richness and detail.
We should all be so lucky to have that kind of love in our lives, whether it comes from one person or more.
The two plays also share some unfortunately flat, at times redundant dialogue, and, under Wills's direction, there are long pauses and indulgent pacing that do little to help the action along.
Jerome has the uncanny feeling of being perfectly adequate in all of its components, but never truly mesmerizing.
The play doesn't really come together, aside from a fantasy sequence in the second act, because there isn't an electricity in their dynamic.
Caswell's unfocused and not always credible play attempts with too little success to incorporate all those plots and more.
A thoughtful and affecting drama about the dead who never entirely leave us
Jerome offers flashes of brilliance, but Caswell's play lacks the narrative cohesion and polish needed to bind its provocative ideas fully.
Impressive stagecraft can't make up for an unconvincing story or characters who seem unlikely to be friends, let alone passionate lovers.

cn.t: This AIDS-era drama set in a ghost town receives a mixed response from critics, who find Caswell's play earnest but uneven in its execution.
